sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ekkeko** ​(*ekkeko*) — ‌Luck, Abundance ‌· The ​dwarf ​— belongs ​to the ​Incan ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued under ​the ‌domain "Luck, ​Abundance". The ‌name ​means "The ‌dwarf"[^1].

**Ekkeko** ​is the ​Andean ​god of ​luck and ​abundance: ‌a smiling ​little man ‌bowed under ​a ‌pack holding ​everything a ‌household ​could wish ‌for. His ​mythology is ​young ‌as myths ‌go — ‌a ​colonial chronicler's ​notice, a ‌founding legend ​printed ​in 1904, ‌and a ​January ​fair where ‌all of ​La Paz ‌buys ​its dreams ​in miniature ​— ​but it ‌rests on ‌burden-carrier figurines ​far ‌older than ​the name.[^2]

​PuniCodex ‌records the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Ekkeko** ‌and ​serves its ‌temple at ​[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/ekkeko/). The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— ​a description ​computed from ‌the ​displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*ekkeko* contains ‌the same ​letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics or ‌special encoding ‌is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sources.citation: Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653), Book XIII — the earliest colonial witness: the household idol Equeco, 'a god of wealth and contentment' loaded with packs and bundles.
Johann Jakob von Tschudi, Reisen durch Südamerika (1866–1869) — 19th-century ethnographic account of the Ekeko household image in Bolivia and Peru.
Antonio Díaz Villamil, Exaltación de la Alasita (1904) — prints the founding legend of Ekeko and Coya in the famine.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Ekkeko** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "The ​dwarf"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Ekkeko** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form *ekkeko* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ​no ‌lost diacritics ‌or ‌encoding transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ​keep ​the original ‌evidence ‌visible. ​The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**e** ​→ **E** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **k** ​→ ​**k** — ​Same
- ‌**k** ​→ **k** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**e** → ​**e** ‌— ‌Same
- **k** ​→ ​**k** ​— Same
- ​**o** ‌→ ‌**o** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/ekkeko/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**ekkeko** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Ekkeko.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Ekkeko" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Ekkeko" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"ekkeko" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Ekkeko ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Ekkeko ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.body:
**Ekkeko** ​is ‌luck, ‌abundance. ​The name ​means ​"The ​dwarf" ​and ‌belongs ​to ​the incan ‌tradition.

### ​Sacred ‌Name

​The ‌restoration ​Ekkeko ​returns the ​figure ​to ​scholarly ‌recognition.

### ​Luck

‌Central ​domain: ‌luck, abundance.

### ​Living ‌Tradition

​Honored ‌in ​incan ​myth, ‌cult, and ‌cultural ‌memory.

### ​Canonical ​Restoration

‌Preserved ​as ​a flagship ‌temple ​with ​its ‌canonical ​scholarly ‌spelling ​and ​supporting evidence.

​The ​domain ‌of ‌luck ​is ‌not ​a modern ​abstraction; ‌it ‌names ‌the ‌sphere ​of ‌influence that ​ancient ​worshippers ​attributed ‌to ​Ekkeko. ​Temples, ​texts, ‌and iconography ​converge ​on ​this ‌sphere, ​even ‌when ​local manifestations ‌differ. ​The ‌PuniCodex ‌restoration ​Ekkeko ​restores ​the name ​that ‌governs ‌the ​domain.

sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Ekkeko ‌place ​luck, abundance ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Ekkeko appears ‌in ​incan ‌tradition as ​luck, ​abundance. ​The name's ​meaning, ​"The ‌dwarf", shapes ​the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

​Devotees and ​later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved Ekkeko ‌in ​ritual, ​text, and ‌iconography, ​ensuring ​the name ‌survived ​into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

The ‌myths ​of ​Ekkeko survive ​in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. ‌Each version ​reflects ​the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ‌— poets, ​priests, ‌philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ​PuniCodex ‌entry does ​not ​privilege ​a single ‌version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Ekkeko ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Ekkeko ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Incan ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Ekkeko, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​luck ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Ekeko ​is the ‌god ‌of wanting ​precisely. ​Where state ​religions ​promise salvation ​and ‌warrior cults ​promise ​glory, he ‌promises the ​small, ‌exact things ​of ‌a life: ​a ​house, a ​harvest, ​a child's ​health, ‌a little ​smoke ‌from a ​clay ‌pipe. His ​liturgy ‌is shopping ​— ‌but shopping ​understood ​as the ‌materialization of ‌hope. ‌To buy ​the ​miniature house ‌is ​to admit ​you ‌want the ​house, ​to say ‌so ​publicly, and ‌to ​give the ​wanting ​a place ​to ‌wait. There ‌is ​a quiet ‌theology ​in that: ​desire is ‌not ‌vain if ‌it ‌is offered; ​it ‌becomes vain ​only ​when it ​is ‌hidden. The ​bowed ​back of ​the ‌figurine completes ​the ​lesson. Abundance, ​in ‌the Andes, ​is ‌not lightning ​from heaven ‌but ​something carried ‌— ‌patiently, humbly, ​load ​by load ​— ​until the ‌pack ‌becomes the ​house.[^1]
